SafeAdapt-Poker: Counterfactual Risk Calibration for Budgeted Adaptation under Opponent Shift

CCS: Computing methodologies Multi-agent reinforcement learningCCS: Computing methodologies Adversarial learningCCS: Information systems Decision support systems
Miaobo Hu1,2, Shuhao Hu2, Xiaobo Guo2, Xin Wang2
Bokun Wang2, Rui Chen2, Daren Zha2, Jun Xiao1,∗
1School of Artificial Intelligence, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China
2Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China
∗Corresponding author: xiaojun@ucas.ac.cn
© none
Abstract.

Repeated interaction exposes public evidence about an opponent, but the same history can become misleading after a behavioral shift. SafeAdapt-Poker formulates budgeted adaptation under opponent shift as a dual-counterfactual sequential-control problem using only information available before each decision. At each decision the controller asks two distinct questions: what local downside a deviation from the frozen anchor would induce under matched legal continuations, and what future adaptation value would be lost by consuming part of the remaining deviation budget now. The first question is answered by a monotone strategic-risk model over deviation intensity; the second by a paired budget-state continuation model that prices current budget consumption. The controller selects among support-preserving candidate deviations by trading immediate adaptation value against these two quantities, a pathwise cumulative-KL ledger bounds total anchor-relative deviation, and a finite family of frozen controllers is screened on complete paired calibration sessions before held-out interaction. A finite-candidate perturbation bound shows that the allocation objective degrades continuously with continuation-value estimation error. Evaluation covers exact-game exploitation and safety, four opponent shifts, local-risk calibration, delayed-opportunity allocation, direct opportunity-value estimation, value-error robustness, factorial mechanism attribution, budget sensitivity, abstract-HUNL cross-play, and player/time-held-out public-history behavior. On exact Leduc the full controller attains a matched weak-pool gain of +0.0718+0.0718 with a worst-opponent delta of −0.0126-0.0126, raises delayed-opportunity capture from 0.6318 under myopic allocation to 0.7841 under the same session budget, and reaches +42.7+42.7 mbb/hand in abstract-HUNL cross-play; the retained public-history screen reports 0.5820 action accuracy and 0.9277 log loss versus 0.5039 and 0.9778 for a public prior.

Keywords: 
Opponent modeling, Safe adaptation, Imperfect-information games, Poker, Multiagent learning

1. Introduction

Poker is a repeated multiagent decision problem: a hero agent chooses legal actions in an imperfect-information game while an opponent agent generates a cross-hand public action history. The hero can exploit recurring behavior, yet must preserve a strong baseline when evidence is sparse, deceptive, or non-stationary (Fudenberg and Levine, 1998). This paper asks: how should an agent spend a bounded amount of deviation from an anchor while adapting only from information observable before the current decision?

Safe opponent exploitation and game-theoretic opponent modeling already show that best responses can be brittle and that equilibrium priors can be updated from action frequencies (Johanson et al., 2007; Johanson and Bowling, 2009; Ganzfried and Sandholm, 2011; Ganzfried and Sandholm, 2015; Liu et al., 2022; Ge et al., 2024). The remaining design issue is session-level control: an adaptation that is locally plausible can accumulate risk across hands or continue trusting a stale history after an opponent shift. Our formulation makes support, uncertainty, shift, and cumulative deviation first-class online state variables.

SafeAdapt-Poker (Figure 1) uses a frozen anchor and a history-conditioned residual: a public-history encoder produces context-conditioned evidence and candidate deviations, legal counterfactual continuations supervise a strategic-risk curve over deviation intensity, and a return-to-go controller uses that curve, remaining KL, and remaining session length to decide whether to spend or retain budget. The selected distribution is projected onto the anchor support and debited from a pathwise ledger, a closed-loop calibration stage evaluates frozen controllers on complete sessions, and policy traces are frozen before any outcome, private-card, or value oracle is joined. As in support-preserving offline RL (Kumar et al., 2020; Kostrikov et al., 2022) and D4RL-style protocols (Fu et al., 2020), the offline controls and player/time splits are fixed in advance.

Two counterfactuals guide allocation. The action counterfactual measures local downside under a matched anchor continuation; the budget-state counterfactual prices future value lost by spending capacity now. SafeAdapt couples these temporal scales through a pathwise KL ledger and a controller family screened on paired sessions before held-out interaction.

Contributions.

(1) Dual-counterfactual formulation of safe adaptation. We formulate repeated opponent adaptation under a finite anchor-relative deviation budget as a sequential allocation problem with two distinct counterfactual estimands: the local strategic downside of an action deviation under a matched anchor continuation, and the continuation value lost by consuming scarce adaptation capacity at the current decision. The separation distinguishes “whether it is locally safe to adapt” from “whether it is worth spending capacity now.” (2) Counterfactual risk–opportunity control. We instantiate the two estimands with a monotone conditional strategic-risk model supervised by legal matched continuations and a paired budget-state continuation model for opportunity-aware allocation, and we bound how continuation-value estimation error propagates to the candidate-selection objective. On exact Leduc the full controller reaches a +0.0718+0.0718 weak-pool gain at a −0.0126-0.0126 worst-opponent delta and captures 0.7841 of delayed high-value opportunities versus 0.6318 for myopic allocation. (3) Multi-scale safety evaluation. One protocol connects decision-level counterfactual calibration, trajectory-level cumulative-KL accounting, and deployment-level finite-family controller selection; its experiments separately test local-risk calibration, opportunity-value estimation and robustness, delayed-opportunity allocation, safety–exploitation trade-offs, four opponent shifts, factorial attribution, abstract-HUNL cross-play, and player/time-held-out public-history generalization.

2. Related Work

Poker agents and anchor policies.

Counterfactual regret minimization and its neural variants provide the standard equilibrium-oriented foundation for small or abstracted imperfect-information games (Zinkevich et al., 2007; Brown et al., 2019; Tammelin, 2014; Brown and Sandholm, 2019a). NFSP and OpenSpiel make population response, self-play, and game instrumentation explicit (Heinrich and Silver, 2016; Lanctot et al., 2019). DeepStack, Libratus, ReBeL, and Pluribus illustrate that strong poker systems additionally require search, abstraction, opponent-pool design, and substantial engineering (Moravčík et al., 2017; Brown and Sandholm, 2018; Brown et al., 2020; Brown and Sandholm, 2019b). Subgame decomposition and refinement are studied in (Burch et al., 2014; Moravčík et al., 2016; Brown and Sandholm, 2017). The present anchor is a frozen reference policy whose strength is measured separately from the adaptation module; this keeps policy-facing observations distinct from evaluation oracles.

Closest safe exploitation and online modeling.

Bayesian modeling and agent-modeling surveys provide complementary foundations (Southey et al., 2005; Albrecht and Stone, 2018; Hernandez-Leal et al., 2019). Restricted Nash Response and Data Biased Robust Counter Strategies balance model exploitation with robustness to inaccurate observations (Johanson et al., 2007; Johanson and Bowling, 2009). Game-theoretic opponent modeling updates an equilibrium prior from action frequencies and recomputes a response online (Ganzfried and Sandholm, 2011), while Safe Opponent Exploitation characterizes worst-case guarantees for adaptive play (Ganzfried and Sandholm, 2015). Safe Exploitation Search (SES) and OX-Search provide online search procedures with explicit exploitability or adaptation-safety analyses (Liu et al., 2022; Ge et al., 2024). A recent learned sequence baseline, StratFormer, couples a transformer opponent model to an exploitability-tied curriculum on Leduc (Caen et al., 2026). SafeAdapt differs in making a public-only session budget and a shift detector part of the policy interface and in separating local intervention risk from the intertemporal value of retained budget (Table 6 in the appendix); the evaluation uses the same anchor-relative estimands for all baselines.

Uncertainty, constraints, and sequential allocation.

Calibration metrics and reliability diagrams are standard tools for separating discrimination from probability quality (Guo et al., 2017; Kull et al., 2019); deep ensembles and shift-aware uncertainty motivate the explicit uncertainty and shift heads (Lakshminarayanan et al., 2017; Ovadia et al., 2019). Constrained MDPs, trust-region updates, and safe policy improvement connect the KL ledger to policy-facing constraints (Altman, 1999; Achiam et al., 2017; Schulman et al., 2015; Schulman et al., 2017; Laroche et al., 2019; Thomas et al., 2015; Chow et al., 2018b). MCCFR, online search, and poker-specific solver work motivate the matched exact-game baselines (Lanctot et al., 2009; Lisý et al., 2015; Schmid et al., 2019; Tammelin et al., 2015; Johanson et al., 2012). The opportunity window is a finite resource-allocation problem (Badanidiyuru et al., 2013; Carrara et al., 2019); complete-hand confidence estimates follow clustered resampling and bounded-difference reasoning (Hoeffding, 1963). Monte Carlo estimation and common-random-number rollouts provide the evaluation precedents for the counterfactual labels (Glasserman, 2004; Yadav et al., 2026), while explicit reward-hacking checks motivate keeping strategic value separate from public-history agreement (Skalse et al., 2022). Sequence-conditioned behavior models and imperfect-information benchmarks built around unseen partners motivate the player/time-held-out history split (Chen et al., 2021; Bard et al., 2020). Public-belief control offers another shared-history precedent (Foerster et al., 2019). The finite deviation budget relates SafeAdapt to constrained sequential decision making, but the allocated object is adaptation capacity relative to a frozen anchor, and SafeAdapt separates two counterfactuals that a single constrained objective conflates: the local downside of changing the current action distribution and the future value lost by changing the remaining-budget state.

Distillation and selective adaptation.

Distillation compresses a teacher policy (Rusu et al., 2016); SafeAdapt instead measures and gates anchor-relative deviation. Selective prediction motivates abstention and coverage (Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2019) for the closed gate, which excludes history from the current action.

3. Method

3.1. Cross-Hand Interaction and Public Information

We consider a two-player imperfect-information game with hands indexed by hh and hero decisions indexed by tt, with h⁡(t)h(t) denoting the hand at decision tt. Let sts_{t} be the hero information state and H<tpubH^{\mathrm{pub}}_{<t} the ordered public history before that decision. The online state is

xt=(st,H<tpub,Bt,ℓt),ℓt=Hmax−h⁡(t)+1,x_{t}=(s_{t},H^{\mathrm{pub}}_{<t},B_{t},\ell_{t}),\qquad\ell_{t}=H_{\max}-h(t)+1,

where BtB_{t} is remaining cumulative KL and ℓt\ell_{t} is the remaining hand horizon. The legal action set is 𝒜⁡(st)\mathcal{A}(s_{t}). A policy may compute zt=fϕ​(H<tpub)z_{t}=f_{\phi}(H^{\mathrm{pub}}_{<t}) and uncertainty utu_{t}, but it cannot use opponent private cards, hidden switch labels, terminal outcomes, or labels revealed only after the current decision. Every hero decision, rather than every hand boundary, consumes the pathwise ledger.

The retained PHH adapter uses a public prior and a count-based history distribution; the strategic controller uses a context-conditioned encoder, candidate residual policies, a risk model, and a budget allocator. In both cases memory is updated only with public events available before a later decision, opponent identity or style, private cards, terminal outcomes, and offline value maps remain post-hoc fields, sequence identifiers route memory resets without serving as predictive features, and the actor-facing state and the scoring state are frozen separately before the oracle join. Appendix B tabulates which fields can influence the adapter at decision time and which values are available only to scoring.

Let 𝒟cal\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{cal}} and 𝒟eval\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{eval}} be calibration and evaluation records. For cross-hand generalization, the opponent ID sets and hand or sequence IDs must be disjoint:

J𝒫​(π)=𝔼o∼𝒫​[EV⁡(π,o)],Δ𝒫​(π,π0)=J𝒫​(π)−J𝒫​(π0).J_{\mathcal{P}}(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{o\sim\mathcal{P}}\left[\operatorname{EV}(\pi,o)\right],\qquad\Delta_{\mathcal{P}}(\pi;\pi_{0})=J_{\mathcal{P}}(\pi)-J_{\mathcal{P}}(\pi_{0}).

The PHH action screen reports behavior-prediction metrics, while matched game studies report these anchor-relative values together with

(1) qh\displaystyle q_{h} =1−exp(−nh/τq),\displaystyle=1-\exp(-n_{h}/\tau_{q}), uh\displaystyle u_{h} ∈[0,1],\displaystyle\in[0,1], dh\displaystyle d_{h} =DJS(precent∥plong),\displaystyle=D_{\mathrm{JS}}(p_{\mathrm{recent}}\,\|\,p_{\mathrm{long}}),

Recovery time is the first hand after a declared shift at which rolling Δ𝒫\Delta_{\mathcal{P}} is positive for KK consecutive hands; post-shift regret and maximum drawdown use the same sequence-level unit.

3.3.4. Dual-Counterfactual Risk and Opportunity Control

The controller separates two interventions with different causal and temporal meanings. The action counterfactual changes the current deviation intensity while holding the subsequent anchor continuation fixed, and measures local strategic downside. The budget-state counterfactual changes only the remaining adaptation capacity supplied to matched future continuations, and measures the intertemporal opportunity cost of spending that capacity. The online controller combines the two quantities but estimates them from separate paired constructions.

For a candidate mixture

πt,η=(1−η)​π0+η​πraw,η∈[0,1],\pi_{t,\eta}=(1-\eta)\pi_{0}+\eta\pi_{\rm raw},\qquad\eta\in[0,1],

The risk head is trained on calibration opponents and frozen before evaluation; local risk remains distinct from session-level downside and exploitability. The constraint encodes the within-state ordering of a common intervention. Predicted risks still vary with public history, support, uncertainty, and shift evidence at the same intensity, through continuation-value supervision.

Let VV denote the true continuation value, Ω⁡(ξt,k)=V⁡(ξt,Bt)−V⁡(ξt,Bt−k)\Omega(\xi_{t},k)=V(\xi_{t},B_{t})-V(\xi_{t},B_{t}-k) the true opportunity cost, and S⁡(j)=g⁡(ξt,j)−Ω⁡(ξt,k¯t​(j))S(j)=g(\xi_{t},j)-\Omega(\xi_{t},\bar{k}_{t}(j)) the true allocation score of candidate jj, with S^​(j)=g^ω​(ξt,j)−Ωω​(ξt,k¯t​(j))\widehat{S}(j)=\widehat{g}_{\omega}(\xi_{t},j)-\Omega_{\omega}(\xi_{t},\bar{k}_{t}(j)) its estimate.

Proposition 3.1.

If |Vω​(ξt,B′)−V⁡(ξt,B′)|≤ϵV|V_{\omega}(\xi_{t},B^{\prime})-V(\xi_{t},B^{\prime})|\leq\epsilon_{V} for every queried budget state B′B^{\prime} and |g^ω​(ξt,j)−g⁡(ξt,j)|≤ϵg|\widehat{g}_{\omega}(\xi_{t},j)-g(\xi_{t},j)|\leq\epsilon_{g} for every j∈𝒥γ​(ξt)j\in\mathcal{J}_{\gamma}(\xi_{t}), then |Ωω​(ξt,k¯t​(j))−Ω⁡(ξt,k¯t​(j))|≤2​ϵV|\Omega_{\omega}(\xi_{t},\bar{k}_{t}(j))-\Omega(\xi_{t},\bar{k}_{t}(j))|\leq 2\epsilon_{V} and the selected candidate satisfies

S⁡(j⋆)−S⁡(jt)≤2​ϵg+4​ϵV,j⋆=arg⁡maxj∈𝒥γ​(ξt)⁡S⁡(j).S(j^{\star})-S(j_{t})\leq 2\epsilon_{g}+4\epsilon_{V},\qquad j^{\star}=\arg\max_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{\gamma}(\xi_{t})}S(j).

The bound follows from the triangle inequality and the argmax perturbation argument over the finite feasible set (Appendix C.1). It is a per-decision statement: the intertemporal allocation objective degrades continuously with the estimation errors of the gain and continuation-value models, which Section 4.8 tests empirically.

Before test interaction, a predeclared finite family of frozen controllers is evaluated on complete paired sessions. For controller cc and calibration group gg, the normalized downside mean μ^c,g\widehat{\mu}_{c,g} and upper bound

Uc,g=μ^c,g+log⁡(2​M​|𝒢|/δ)2​ngU_{c,g}=\widehat{\mu}_{c,g}+\sqrt{\frac{\log(2M|\mathcal{G}|/\delta)}{2n_{g}}}

are computed from independent blocks; a controller is retained only when maxg⁡Uc,g≤ρ\max_{g}U_{c,g}\leq\rho. The grids, tie-break rule, label-generation cost, and rejected-candidate counts are fixed before held-out evaluation and recorded in Appendix D.

3.3.5. Pathwise KL Ledger and Heuristic Projection

The product allowance below is the fixed-module heuristic baseline, called Heuristic SafeAdapt; the learned allocator selects among the same projected candidates. With BtB_{t} the remaining session budget (B1=BB_{1}=B), the heuristic allowance is δtheur=min⁡{Bt,δmax​qt​(1−ut)​(1−dt)}\delta_{t}^{\rm heur}=\min\{B_{t},\delta_{\max}q_{t}(1-u_{t})(1-d_{t})\}, and the mixture πη=(1−η)​π0+η​πraw\pi_{\eta}=(1-\eta)\pi_{0}+\eta\pi_{\mathrm{raw}} (or ptp_{t} for the count baseline) is projected by the same one-dimensional binary search as above with δtheur\delta_{t}^{\rm heur} in place of δKL\delta_{\mathrm{KL}}, giving ηt⋆\eta_{t}^{\star}. The ledger is debited after the distribution is fixed:

Bt+1=Bt−k¯t,k¯t≥DKL(πηt⋆∥π0),∑tk¯t≤B.B_{t+1}=B_{t}-\overline{k}_{t},\qquad\overline{k}_{t}\geq D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\eta_{t}^{\star}}\|\pi_{0}),\qquad\sum_{t}\overline{k}_{t}\leq B.

When Bt=0B_{t}=0 or dtd_{t} crosses its validation threshold, the action distribution is π0\pi_{0} and the fast summary is refreshed without replenishing BtB_{t}; the budget sweep in Section 4 makes projection activity observable rather than inferred from a non-binding radius.

3.3.6. Trajectory-Level Anchor-Deviation Analysis

Proposition 3.2.

If SafeAdapt and the anchor use the same chance and opponent kernels and the session KL ledger is at most BB, the chain rule gives

DKL(PSA(τ)∥P0(τ))≤B.D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{\mathrm{SA}}(\tau)\|P_{0}(\tau))\leq B.

For a bounded return G⁡(τ)∈[−U,U]G(\tau)\in[-U,U], Pinsker’s inequality then yields

|Jo​(πSA)−Jo​(π0)|≤U​2​B.\left|J_{o}(\pi_{\mathrm{SA}})-J_{o}(\pi_{0})\right|\leq U\sqrt{2B}.

The proof of Proposition 3.2 applies the KL chain rule to the decision kernels and bounds the difference of bounded expectations by total variation (Cover and Thomas, 2006). The statement is an anchor-deviation certificate under its declared kernel and budget conditions; EV, best-response, and exploitability are measured separately.

3.3.7. Leakage-Free Execution Contract

The experiment follows one frozen ordering: label generation, tuning and calibration, controller selection, online interaction, and post-trace scoring; diagnostic screens are reported separately. (1) The anchor, action vocabulary, legal-action mask, resource ledger, and opponent-pool split are frozen before any adapter is fitted. (2) Calibration uses only public actions from calibration hands and is frozen, with a recorded digest, before held-out sequences are evaluated. (3) At each decision the controller serializes the hero state and public history, computes qt,ut,dtq_{t},u_{t},d_{t}, scores candidates with r^t​j\widehat{r}_{tj}, allocates jtj_{t}, verifies and debits k¯t\overline{k}_{t} from BtB_{t}, and records the action. (4) Memory receives only actions that are public before a later decision, never the current action label, private cards, terminal outcome, or offline value map. (5) The residual is trained on weak-pool value with mean, CVaR, and worst-case constraints checked on a separate validation pool; all seeds and failures are retained. (6) Value or historical-action oracles are joined only after the trace is immutable; every deterministic trace is replayed, and all failures are published.

4. Experiments

4.1. Experimental Setup and Research Questions

The experiments address nine questions: weak-opponent value (RQ1), mean and tail safety (RQ2), recovery under four opponent shifts (RQ3), held-out counterfactual-risk calibration (RQ4), delayed-opportunity budget allocation (RQ5), factorial attribution of risk and opportunity value (RQ6), player/time-held-out generalization and large-game cross-play (RQ7), direct estimation quality of the budget-opportunity counterfactual (RQ8), and robustness to continuation-value error and unseen opportunity timing (RQ9). The execution order follows Section 3.3.7. The statistical unit is the opponent–sequence–seed block in exact Leduc and the opponent–deal–seed block in abstract HUNL. All adaptive baselines receive matched current-hand information, public history, legal-action masks, anchor checkpoints, action vocabularies, and interaction budgets. Search and learned baselines use matched solver calls and environment steps. Appendix D fixes the estimands and units before measurement; intervals resample complete blocks. Unless a caption states otherwise, bold and underline mark the best and second-best comparable entries.

Table 1 compares the safety–exploitation frontier across adaptive baselines under a fixed anchor, opponent pool, seat protocol, solver configuration, and statistical unit. Full SafeAdapt attains a weak-pool gain of +0.0718±0.0058+0.0718\pm 0.0058, second only to the naive best response (+0.1102+0.1102), while holding worst-opponent degradation to −0.0126±0.0029-0.0126\pm 0.0029 against −0.1846-0.1846 for the naive best response and −0.0298-0.0298 for OX-Search, the strongest search baseline; its snapshot exploitability (0.0264) and recovery time (8.9 hands) are the lowest among adaptive methods, and the heuristic controller lies between OX-Search and the full controller in every column, so the learned risk curve and opportunity value add safety and recovery speed beyond the product-rule allowance.

4.2. Counterfactual Risk Calibration

Study RQ4 tests whether legal matched continuations improve the local strategic-downside estimate beyond action counts or generic uncertainty. For each held-out public state, candidate deviation intensities are fixed before a continuation oracle is joined, and Yt​j=𝟏{ηt​jLt<−ϵloc}Y_{tj}=\mathbf{1}\{\eta_{tj}L_{t}<-\epsilon_{\mathrm{loc}}\} is the target. We compare count support, uncertainty-only, a product heuristic, an unconstrained classifier, and the monotone counterfactual-risk curve, fitted only on the calibration split.

The monotone counterfactual-risk curve reaches AUROC 0.8819 and AUPRC 0.7886 against 0.8147 and 0.7118 for the unconstrained classifier, and lowers ECE from 0.0594 to 0.0318 and accepted downside from 0.0201 to 0.0119; count support and uncertainty-only models trail on every metric (Table 2). The improvement therefore concerns probability quality and the downside actually admitted by the feasible set, not only ranking. Stratification by deviation intensity and by shift condition is reported in Appendix D.

4.3. Opponent Shift and Recovery

Study RQ3 evaluates stationary controls and four predeclared shifts: abrupt tight-to-loose, reverse aggressive-to-passive, gradual drift over 20–40 hands, and bait-and-switch. The switch hand is fixed before tuning; recovery hands count the first post-switch hand followed by KK consecutive hands with positive rolling anchor-relative value, and sessions that never recover are right-censored.

Figure 2 summarizes the four shifts. Full SafeAdapt has the lowest post-shift regret and the fastest recovery in every condition. Under the bait-and-switch schedule, the hardest case for history-based exploitation, its regret is 0.0578±0.00660.0578\pm 0.0066 against 0.09630.0963 for OX-Search and 0.17840.1784 for count statistics, and it recovers in 11.9 hands versus 22.5 and 41.7; across conditions its shift-detection AUROC ranges from 0.856 (gradual drift) to 0.902 (bait-and-switch) and its maximum drawdown from 0.0237 to 0.0409, while StratFormer, the learned sequence baseline, recovers between 16.9 and 27.4 hands (Table 9).

4.4. Safety–Exploitation Frontier and Ablations

The budget sweep (RQ1–RQ2) moves the session budget from anchor-only to unconstrained and records projection activity, mean KL, weak-pool gain, and worst degradation (Figure 3; values in Table 8 in the appendix). Weak-pool gain rises from +0.0258+0.0258 under the very small budget, where 78.4% of decisions are projected, to +0.0754+0.0754 under the large budget (24.2% projected), while worst-opponent degradation grows from −0.0047-0.0047 to −0.0196-0.0196; removing the ledger reaches +0.1037+0.1037 but costs −0.0915-0.0915 against the worst opponent, so the ledger removes most of the worst-case loss for a much smaller reduction in gain. Each component ablation is retrained with the same initialization family, opponent pool, environment steps, optimizer budget, and independent seeds.

4.5. Delayed-Opportunity Budget Allocation

Study RQ5 creates an early window with frequent low-value deviations and a later window with rarer high-value opportunities; opponent schedule, chance outcomes, candidate menu, and total session KL are shared across methods, and the offline oracle is joined after online traces are frozen as an upper-bound diagnostic. Early KL is the fraction spent before the high-value window, BoppB_{\mathrm{opp}} the remaining budget at that window, and capture the fraction of high-value decisions at which sufficient budget remains.

Full SafeAdapt spends 0.2153 of its budget before the high-value window against 0.3281 for the myopic controller and 0.4813 for the fixed-KL residual, retains 0.5932 of the budget at the window, and captures 0.7841 of high-value decisions versus 0.6318 and 0.4162; its session gain (+0.0698+0.0698) and worst delta (−0.0131-0.0131) are the closest to the offline oracle (+0.0837+0.0837, −0.0094-0.0094). The heuristic and myopic controllers improve on the fixed-KL residual but still spend budget early, which is the behavior the opportunity value is designed to remove (Table 3).

Removing the history representation forfeits most of the gain (+0.0183+0.0183), removing the shift detector or the cumulative ledger inflates worst-opponent loss to −0.0358-0.0358 and −0.0506-0.0506 with recovery slowing to 24.9 and 18.7 hands, and the count-gated baseline recovers in 26.4 hands; the full controller is the only variant with a worst delta above −0.02-0.02 and recovery below 10 hands (Table 10 in the appendix).

4.6. Factorial Mechanism Attribution

Study RQ6 holds the history encoder, residual policy, shift detector, candidate menu, pathwise ledger, initialization family, environment-step budget, and opponent splits fixed while toggling the two proposed mechanisms. The risk-only arm uses the learned risk curve with a myopic feasible-set controller; the budget-value-only arm uses the learned opportunity value with the fixed heuristic risk filter. The four cells share the same seeds and paired blocks and are compared within the table.

Risk supervision alone moves the worst-opponent delta from −0.0468-0.0468 to −0.0201-0.0201 and recovery from 24.7 to 12.2 hands while delayed capture improves only to 0.5294; opportunity value alone raises capture to 0.6961 with a smaller safety change (−0.0287-0.0287); both together reach the best value in every column (+0.0718+0.0718, −0.0126-0.0126, 8.9 hands, 0.7841). The two mechanisms therefore act on different estimands, safety and recovery for the risk curve and intertemporal capture for the opportunity value, and their combination is a Pareto improvement over either alone (Table 4).

4.7. Budget-Opportunity Estimation Quality

Study RQ8 evaluates the opportunity-value model independently of downstream policy return: for each held-out decision state, the public state, candidate debit, opponent mechanism, and chance realization are frozen, and two matched continuations that differ only in remaining budget supply the reference opportunity target. We report absolute opportunity-cost error, rank correlation across candidate debits, pairwise ranking accuracy (the quantity the controller consumes), and the regret of selecting a candidate with the estimated rather than the reference cost, against an unpaired continuation-value regressor and an independent-rollout difference that shares neither chance nor opponent realization across the two budget states.

The paired budget-state estimator reduces opportunity-cost MAE from 0.0335 for independent-rollout differences to 0.0182 and allocation regret from 0.0152 to 0.0068, while raising rank correlation from 0.6841 to 0.8463 and pairwise ranking accuracy from 0.7815 to 0.8974 (Table 15). Shared chance and opponent realizations improve the candidate ordering used by the allocator.

4.8. Opportunity-Value Robustness

Study RQ9 tests the sensitivity predicted by Proposition 3.1: zero-mean perturbations, scaled by the standard deviation of the held-out opportunity targets, are injected into the frozen opportunity-value predictions at evaluation time while all other inputs, the KL budget, and every model stay fixed. The same protocol relocates the high-value window to timing conditions excluded from training (Table 14 in the appendix).

From zero to large value noise, early KL rises from 0.2153 to 0.3018, capture falls from 0.7841 to 0.6627, session gain declines from +0.0698+0.0698 to +0.0609+0.0609, and worst-opponent delta changes from −0.0131-0.0131 to −0.0174-0.0174 (Table 16). The large-noise controller retains a better value in all four metrics than myopic allocation (Table 3). Under held-out timing, the full controller exceeds myopic gain in all five conditions, including +0.0228+0.0228 on the unseen bursty schedule (Table 14).

4.9. Large-Game Cross-Play

The scalability study fixes an abstract HUNL configuration before evaluation (abstractions, anchor, opponent families, duplicate deals, seat swaps, LBR evaluator, and matched budgets; Appendix D) and reports mbb/hand, opponent LBR payoff, and strong-pool and worst-opponent degradation.

Full SafeAdapt reaches +42.7±3.3+42.7\pm 3.3 mbb/hand with the lowest opponent LBR payoff (34.2, below the anchor’s 42.6) and the smallest strong-pool and worst-opponent degradation (−4.8-4.8 and −9.6-9.6 mbb/hand); OX-Search, the strongest search baseline, attains +34.2+34.2 at −17.2-17.2 worst-opponent degradation, and StratFormer trades +38.5+38.5 for −28.3-28.3 (Table 5). Counterfactual labels are generated offline and the deployed controller evaluates only the frozen history, risk, and opportunity models; label-generation and training hours, online latency, and peak memory are in Table 19 in the appendix.

4.10. Real PHH History Generalization

The eight-entry PHH fixture (36 calibration and 43 evaluation hands from disjoint player-set and time groups, with a frozen manifest and replay check) gives safe history 0.5820 action accuracy and 0.9277 log loss against 0.5039 and 0.9778 for the public prior (Table 22 in the appendix). Claims about public-history generalization use the complete-entry evaluation with 41,817 calibration and 54,556 evaluation snapshots in a fixed split order; confidence intervals resample complete hands at player-set or time-group level, and Table 21 in the appendix reports paired safe-history-minus-control intervals for the Laplace-smoothed count baseline and the full method.

Across complete-hand clusters, safe history improves player-set accuracy by +0.0716+0.0716 and time-group accuracy by +0.0579+0.0579 with paired intervals that exclude zero, lowers log loss, Brier score, and ECE, raises shift AUROC from 0.6412 to 0.8127, and halves the false-adaptation rate (Table 21).

5. Limitations, Ethics, and Conclusion

Construct and internal validity.

Historical action agreement measures recorded public actions, whereas strategic value is measured by the paired game estimands in Tables 1 and 5; the tiny-Leduc diagnostic uses an analytic style-conditioned scorer and a finite declared policy. The retained history adapter is frequency-based and bucketed, whereas the full method adds a learned sequence representation, uncertainty heads, a shift branch, and gradient-trained residuals with independent seeds; because snapshots within a hand are clustered, intervals resample complete hand groups and opponent–sequence blocks.

External validity and leakage.

The eight-entry PHH screen is a deterministic replay fixture; generalization claims use the complete-entry audit, whose variation is limited to the recorded stakes, sites, human play, and time groups, while tiny Leduc and abstract HUNL cover the declared finite-game and action-space settings. Current actions, private cards, outcomes, styles, and value maps stay outside the online trace, and a replay check mutates each oracle field and compares the resulting policy trace before the post-trace join.

Calibration, estimator, and label dependence.

The finite-family calibration proposition is a selection-time statement under the declared calibration-session distribution; its group-wise bound can deteriorate for opponents outside the covered mechanisms, so held-out worst-opponent value and shift experiments remain separate evidence. Risk supervision uses exact legal continuations in the finite game and a declared rollout and abstraction procedure in HUNL. Proposition 3.1 bounds the selection error under uniform continuation-value error, but systematic out-of-distribution error can still cause premature spending or excessive budget retention; opportunity-target prediction, ranking accuracy, value-noise sensitivity, held-out timing, and label cost are therefore reported separately from policy return.

Ethics and release.

The PHH source is accessed from PokerHandHistory.com (https://www.pokerhandhistory.com/), retrieved 2026-09-28; raw hands are not redistributed and use follows the site’s public terms. The policy uses public observations, private cards and identity remain post-hoc, and the anonymous release excludes identifying metadata, host paths, secrets, weights, and large caches.

Conclusion.

SafeAdapt-Poker casts opponent adaptation as dual-counterfactual sequential control under finite anchor-relative capacity: the action counterfactual estimates the local downside of changing the current distribution, the budget-state counterfactual estimates the future value lost by consuming capacity now, the pathwise ledger bounds the sequence, and closed-loop calibration selects among frozen controllers before held-out interaction. Matched experiments connect these mechanisms to calibration, opportunity allocation, shift recovery, cross-play, and held-out public-history behavior, with exploitability and worst-opponent value measured separately from the anchor-deviation certificate.

Appendix A Closest-Work Comparison

Table 6 compares SafeAdapt-Poker with the safe exploitation and online opponent-modeling methods discussed in Section 2. The search-based methods provide explicit safety for each computed response, and StratFormer regularizes a learned sequence model toward low exploitability; none of them carries a session-level deviation ledger. SafeAdapt-Poker combines a public-only sequence input, an explicit shift mechanism, and a cumulative anchor-relative budget, and all methods in the table are evaluated with the same anchor-relative estimands.

Appendix B Safety Conditions and Information Boundary

B.1. Safety Conditions

  • •

    The online state contains only information available before the current decision; hidden opponent cards and terminal outcomes remain offline.

  • •

    Calibration, threshold selection, and anchor selection occur before held-out opponent evaluation.

  • •

    The anchor, action support, rollout budget, and scorer are fixed across policy comparisons.

  • •

    Report strong-pool mean, worst-opponent degradation, and weak-pool gain as separate opponent-pool quantities.

  • •

    Action agreement, exact analytic utility, and strategic EV are separate metrics with separate labels.

  • •

    Duplicate hands, seat balancing, switch controls, and clustered intervals precede a poker-strength claim.

  • •

    Solver, model, and deployment evidence are recorded as measured fields.

B.2. Information Boundary

Table 7 lists the policy-facing and post-hoc fields enforced by these conditions.

Appendix C Strategic Evaluation Definitions

Snapshot NashConv and exploitability.

The frozen single-hand policy is queried at every legal information set under the declared chance and opponent kernels. For history-conditioned controllers a snapshot additionally requires a controller context: before evaluation we freeze the public-history prefix, remaining budget, uncertainty state, shift state, and all recurrent summaries associated with each queried snapshot, and every method is evaluated on the same predeclared snapshot contexts. Best-response queries may vary the legal hero action but cannot mutate these frozen cross-hand controller variables. Snapshot NashConv is the sum of each player’s unilateral best-response improvement values under that profile, and the reported exploitability is snapshot NashConv divided by two for the two-player normalization; it measures the exploitability of the induced single-hand policy conditional on a fixed controller context, while repeated-session value is measured by the session estimands.

Repeated sessions and pools.

The repeated-session estimand runs the complete budget-state controller against a held-out opponent pool with public-history updates, pathwise debits, and post-switch scoring. Recovery is the first post-switch hand followed by the predeclared KK-hand positive rolling anchor-relative-value criterion; runs that never recover are right-censored and reported separately.

C.1. Proof of the Finite-Candidate Perturbation Bound

The opportunity-cost estimate is the difference of two continuation values, so the triangle inequality gives |Ωω−Ω|≤|Vω​(ξt,Bt)−V⁡(ξt,Bt)|+|Vω​(ξt,Bt−k)−V⁡(ξt,Bt−k)|≤2​ϵV|\Omega_{\omega}-\Omega|\leq|V_{\omega}(\xi_{t},B_{t})-V(\xi_{t},B_{t})|+|V_{\omega}(\xi_{t},B_{t}-k)-V(\xi_{t},B_{t}-k)|\leq 2\epsilon_{V}. Consequently |S^​(j)−S⁡(j)|≤ϵg+2​ϵV|\widehat{S}(j)-S(j)|\leq\epsilon_{g}+2\epsilon_{V} uniformly over the finite feasible set 𝒥γ​(ξt)\mathcal{J}_{\gamma}(\xi_{t}), which both maximizations share. Writing e=ϵg+2​ϵVe=\epsilon_{g}+2\epsilon_{V} and using that jtj_{t} maximizes S^\widehat{S},

S⁡(j⋆)−S⁡(jt)\displaystyle S(j^{\star})-S(j_{t}) =[S⁡(j⋆)−S^​(j⋆)]+[S^​(j⋆)−S^​(jt)]\displaystyle=[S(j^{\star})-\widehat{S}(j^{\star})]+[\widehat{S}(j^{\star})-\widehat{S}(j_{t})]
+[S^​(jt)−S⁡(jt)]≤e+0+e,\displaystyle+[\widehat{S}(j_{t})-S(j_{t})]\leq e+0+e,

which gives S⁡(j⋆)−S⁡(jt)≤2​ϵg+4​ϵVS(j^{\star})-S(j_{t})\leq 2\epsilon_{g}+4\epsilon_{V}. The statement is a per-decision perturbation bound over the estimated feasible set; risk-feasibility errors enter only through that set and are evaluated separately by the calibration study.

C.2. Reproducibility Fields

Source binding.

PHH and PokerKit provide standardized recording and simulation interfaces (Kim, 2024; Kim, 2025).

The release package records source-relative configuration, selection, calibration digests, counterfactual-labelled states, candidate intensities, label-generation cost, and controller-family grids without exposing repository paths, host names, commit identifiers, or user metadata. The stability audit remains separate from the primary PHH table; full calibration fields are listed in Appendix D.

Split and oracle integrity.

The eight selected PHH entries are fixed before the snapshot cap, with disjoint calibration/evaluation hands, player-set groups, and time groups. Train-only calibration and frozen online traces are checked before oracle joins. Online traces and oracle artifacts stay separate, and replay checks cover both policy traces and exact rollouts where applicable.

Statistics and cost.

Seeds 13, 17, and 23 are recorded for the protocol. The frozen configuration uses a two-layer encoder (hidden 192), action head 128, uncertainty head 96, shift head 96, dropout 0.10, AdamW at 3×10−43\times 10^{-4}, KL cap δmax=0.08\delta_{\max}=0.08, session budgets {0,0.01,0.02,0.04,0.08,∞}\{0,0.01,0.02,0.04,0.08,\infty\}, temperature 1.37, and gate 0.41. The session ledger measures cumulative KL deviation; GPU time, wall-clock latency, throughput, memory occupancy, and monetary cost are separate fields.

Appendix D Additional Experimental Protocols

This appendix specifies the controlled experiments and statistical units required to attribute the two counterfactual mechanisms. Each table states its protocol and statistical unit before its values so that the estimand is fixed independently of the measured outcome.

D.1. Session-Budget Sweep

Table 8 lists the values plotted in Figure 3. Projection activity is the fraction of decisions whose raw distribution violates the active allowance; the unit is the opponent–sequence–seed block, and every budget level uses the same anchor, opponent pool, and seeds.

D.2. Opponent-Shift Recovery Values

Table 9 lists the post-shift regret, maximum drawdown, recovery hands, and shift-detection AUROC summarized in Figure 2. Recovery hands count the first post-switch hand followed by KK consecutive hands with positive rolling anchor-relative value; right-censored sessions are retained in the failure ledger.

D.3. Component Ablation Values

Table 10 lists the component ablation discussed in Section 4.4; every row is retrained independently under the matched Leduc protocol, and the two counterfactual mechanisms are attributed separately in Table 4.

D.4. Counterfactual Risk Calibration

Table 2 reports the held-out calibration comparison: candidate deviation intensities are frozen before the continuation oracle is joined, the target is Yt​j=𝟏{ηt​jLt<−ϵloc}Y_{tj}=\mathbf{1}\{\eta_{tj}L_{t}<-\epsilon_{\mathrm{loc}}\}, and all metrics use held-out opponent–sequence–seed blocks.

Calibration across deviation intensity.

Because the risk model exploits a known within-state ordering over deviation intensity, held-out candidates are additionally stratified by intervention magnitude. Table 11 reports calibration error and accepted downside for the unconstrained classifier and the monotone model in each stratum, together with the fraction of within-state candidate pairs whose unconstrained predictions violate the monotone ordering; the overall row restates the aggregate values of Table 2. Structurally monotone models provide precedents for enforcing such ordering (Sill, 1997; Daniels and Velikova, 2010).

Figure 4 plots the three strata of Table 11: the monotone model lowers ECE by 45–49% and accepted downside by 40–43% in every stratum, while the unconstrained classifier’s order-violation rate rises from 0.1148 to 0.1834 with intensity.

Risk calibration is also stratified by the predeclared shift schedule in Table 12, whose stationary row coincides with the counterfactual-risk row of the main comparison.

D.5. Delayed-Opportunity Budget Allocation

Each session contains an early phase with frequent low-value deviations and a later phase with rarer high-value deviations. Opponent schedule, chance outcomes, candidate menu, and total KL budget are shared across methods. The oracle allocator is joined only after online traces are frozen and is reported as an upper-bound diagnostic. Early KL is the fraction spent before the high-value window; capture rate is the fraction of high-value decisions at which sufficient budget remains. Figure 5 plots the three allocation quantities of Table 3.

Timing sensitivity.

Table 13 relocates the high-value window within the schedule family used for training. The full controller’s margin over the myopic controller grows from +0.0037+0.0037 for an early window to +0.0303+0.0303 for a late window, matching the intended role of retained budget.

Generalization across opportunity timing.

To distinguish learned budget valuation from memorization of a fixed schedule, the opportunity-value model is retrained without access to the held-out timing condition, and evaluation then relocates the high-value window while preserving the opponent family, total KL budget, candidate menu, and matched chance realizations; the randomized and bursty conditions are never used as training schedules. The full controller retains positive gain margins in all five conditions: +0.0037+0.0037 for early opportunities, +0.0299+0.0299 for late opportunities, and +0.0228+0.0228 for unseen bursty timing (Table 14).

Figure 6 shows the same comparison: the margin is largest when the high-value window comes late (+0.0299+0.0299) and remains +0.0228+0.0228 on the bursty schedule that was never used for training.

D.6. Opportunity-Value Estimation and Robustness

Tables 15 and 16 report the direct estimation quality of the budget-opportunity target (Section 4.7) and the sensitivity of the frozen controller to injected opportunity-value error (Section 4.8); both use the delayed-opportunity protocol and the opponent–sequence–seed block as the unit, and the estimator rows share the held-out decision states, candidate debits, opponent mechanisms, and chance realizations. Regression calibration provides complementary uncertainty diagnostics (Kuleshov et al., 2018).

The noise study perturbs only the frozen opportunity-value predictions; the zero-noise row therefore coincides with the full controller of the delayed-opportunity study, and each larger scale is a multiple of the held-out target standard deviation.

Figure 7 plots the values in Table 16: larger perturbations increase early spending and reduce capture, weak-pool gain, and worst-opponent value.

D.7. Closed-Loop Controller Calibration Audit

The controller family is the predeclared Cartesian product of risk thresholds, session budgets, and strong/tail penalty weights. Every candidate is frozen before complete calibration sessions are evaluated. We report calibration downside, group-wise upper confidence bound, acceptance, held-out downside, and threshold violations (Table 17); held-out results do not change the family or threshold.

Controller-family sensitivity.

Table 18 varies the size of the predeclared frozen family while holding the calibration-session budget fixed, so that the family-wise confidence correction is measured as a selection cost rather than treated only as a formal safeguard. From 16 to 128 candidates, the calibration worst UCB rises from 0.0468 to 0.0538 while the accepted fraction falls from 13/16 to 87/128; weak EV rises from +0.0684+0.0684 to +0.0722+0.0722, and evaluation violations remain zero.

D.8. Abstract-HUNL Configuration and Cost Ledger

The large-game configuration is frozen before evaluation. We record the action abstraction (4 sizes, FCPA), card abstraction (169/1326/2652 buckets), frozen CFR HUNL anchor (2 000 000 steps), held-out pool (12 opponents from 4 families, 1024 duplicate deals, and seat swaps), and matched compute (solver 50 000 calls at 8.2 ms; learned 500 000 interactions and 5 seeds). Opponent LBR uses 10 000 rollouts per state; counterfactual labels use 5 000 rollouts per candidate with a 5% lower-confidence correction. Table 19 reports the label-generation, training, online-latency, and peak-memory fields.

D.9. Controller Family and Reproducibility Fields

The release records the number of labelled states, candidate intensities, exact-tree or rollout calls per candidate, label-generation time, risk-model training time, and the independent validation split used to select ϵloc\epsilon_{\mathrm{loc}} and γ\gamma. The base controller grid contains 36 frozen candidates formed from γ∈{0.05,0.10,0.15,0.20}\gamma\in\{0.05,0.10,0.15,0.20\}, B∈{0.01,0.02,0.04}B\in\{0.01,0.02,0.04\}, and penalty weights {0.5,1.0,2.0}\{0.5,1.0,2.0\}. The calibration threshold is ρ=0.08\rho=0.08 with family-wise confidence 1−δ=0.951-\delta=0.95; ties are broken by lowest_risk fixed before held-out evaluation.

D.10. Completed Experiments and Public-History Fixture

Table 20 lists the completed diagnostics and the matched-study summary.

The release ledger binds each row to a frozen configuration, source digest, selected-entry digest, replay record, and calibration record. Measured diagnostic rows are kept separate from the matched strategic studies.

Public-history generalization.

Table 21 lists the complete-entry behavior metrics summarized in Section 4.10; accuracy is an auxiliary descriptive measure, and the paired intervals are computed on complete-hand clusters.

Public-history fixture.

Table 22 reports behavior agreement on the eight-entry fixture; current actions and raise buckets are post-hoc historical labels, and strategic value is measured by the matched game studies.

Entry-split stability audit.

A separate stability run reloads all 41,817 calibration and 54,556 evaluation snapshots from the same explicit entries, resamples complete hands over four player-set and two time-group evaluation groups for 1,000 deterministic bootstrap replicates, and reproduces the paired intervals of Table 21; the bootstrap action accuracy of safe history is 0.5211 [0.4648, 0.5791] on the player-set axis and 0.5762 [0.5703, 0.5820] on the time-group axis, and replay passes.

Appendix E Finite-Game Diagnostic

E.1. Evaluation Protocol

The held-out run uses a frozen manifest and deterministic replay. It uses three train and three held-out opponent IDs, with styles from the declared passive, aggressive, mixed, tight, and loose catalog. Each opponent contributes 16 ordered hands under a no-switch condition and a switch-at-hand-8 condition, yielding 96 train and 96 held-out rows per seed. Seeds are 13, 17, and 23. The public trace contains an opaque sequence ID, hand index, hero/public state, observed action history, controller state, and ledger fields. Opponent identity, style, private card, and analytic weak and strong values are stored only in the oracle artifact.

Figure 8 visualizes the paired weak-gain and worst-strong trade-off for the retained finite-game diagnostic; the error bars are the same descriptive intervals reported in Table 23.

The exact scorer freezes the hero distribution before expanding chance and opponent transitions, enumerates the finite tiny-Leduc tree with a fail-closed node limit of 4096, and uses the declared opponent policy. Trace, exact-rollout, and combined replay checks pass for this run.

E.2. Diagnostic Results

Table 23 summarizes the held-out trade-off; its intervals describe the fixed fixture, and the strategic tables use the matched-study protocol described above.

The finite-game diagnostic meets its declared utility criteria: each adaptive policy has a positive held-out weak-gain lower interval and the safe-gate worst-opponent lower interval remains above the predeclared −ϵ-\epsilon boundary with ϵ=0.05\epsilon=0.05. The stats policy has the largest weak-proxy gain and the largest strong-proxy degradation among the adaptive rows; the gated policy shows the intended descriptive trade-off. Exact utilities are negative on the fixed contribution states, so their ordering is reported as an analytic diagnostic. The switch-condition rows define the protocol; recovery time is evaluated in the independent shift study.
